## `tests/cell_verify.rs`

### tests/cell_verify.rs:76

````text
There is no "user grid precision" in the OpenAccess API.
````

### tests/cell_verify.rs:95

````text
The four-argument form of dbOpenCellViewByType returns a WINDOW id,
not a cellview, and every accessor on a window id reads nil — so the
audit would report "no drift" for every cellview.
````

### tests/cell_verify.rs:129

````text
The close is the cleanup form of unwindProtect, so it also runs when
the audit raises — a bare trailing dbClose would leak the cellview.
````

### tests/cell_verify.rs:161

````text
The SKILL builds one (layer on off) entry per LAYER and appends the
tails section. These are the fragments that decide the format the
parser has to read.
````

### tests/cell_verify.rs:177

````text
... and the parser reads exactly that: a three-element layer tuple
and the tails marker.
````

### tests/cell_verify.rs:198

````text
497 shapes in the cellview, every one of them on-grid.
````

### tests/cell_verify.rs:226

````text
The live output of the same cellview: it has no supply net, so the
tails section is present and empty. An empty section must not be
mistaken for a layer, and must not make the audit look like it found
something.
````

### tests/cell_verify.rs:239

````text
The tails marker is emitted as a quoted SKILL string, so the parser
has to match on the string value. When it matched on the atom type
instead, the tails entry was read as a layer called "tails".
````

### tests/cell_verify.rs:252

````text
The drift verdict is the sum of the off column, so the counts have to
be per layer and not per shape.
````

### tests/cell_verify.rs:265

````text
A cellview with no shapes still produces a well-formed result: the
SKILL always emits the tails section.
````

### tests/cell_verify.rs:277

````text
A layer entry that is not the three-element (layer on off) tuple.
````

### tests/cell_verify.rs:279

````text
A count that is not a number.
````

### tests/cell_verify.rs:288

````text
SKILL can print a count that went through arithmetic as "3.0".
````

### tests/daemon_user_guard.rs:298

````text
Slice the `"ping"` arm up to the next match arm. Dispatcher arms are
indented 12 spaces, while the payload/comment lines inside an arm are
deeper, so this boundary cannot leak into the following arm — and it
stays correct no matter how long the comment block above the call grows.
````

### tests/daemon_user_guard.rs:310

````text
The actual SKILL payload must be `plus(1 1)`, pinned by exact call form
rather than by any occurrence (the comments above also mention it).
Since step 6c-2 the ping goes through `execute_skill_idempotent_probe`
so that it survives a stale queued ticket — pinning the probe form also
guards against silently reverting to the non-idempotent call.
````

### tests/daemon_user_guard.rs:320

````text
Negative check: the SKILL payload must NOT be the broken call. We allow
the comment to mention ipcIsProcessRunning (for context); the payload is
a quoted string literal, so matching the leading quote keeps this from
firing on the comment.
````

### tests/daemon_user_guard.rs:355

````text
We can't easily construct a real VirtuosoClient without a tunnel
(we'd need an SSHClient). The local-mode branch of ensure_remote_dir
just calls std::fs::create_dir_all — replicate that here and assert
the side effect, so the test is independent of the SSH machinery.
````

### tests/daemon_user_guard.rs:380

````text
Pointing the cache to a non-writable path should NOT panic — the
contract is "best-effort, errors silently ignored".
````

### tests/maestro_jobs.rs:237

````text
Two submits can be handed the same run id. The first submitter owns
it; the later record is the duplicate. The store must name the owner
deterministically, not "whichever the newest-first list happens to
produce".
````

### tests/maestro_jobs.rs:284


### tests/maestro_jobs.rs:309

````text
The job record is the only proof that the job was submitted, so a
reader must never see it disappear while it is being replaced. The
old save removed the destination and renamed the temporary file in
its place, which opens exactly that window.
````

````text
Byte slices: `i` walks raw bytes and may sit inside a multi-byte
UTF-8 character, so slicing the &str would panic.
````

### tests/skill_paren_balance.rs:311

````text
A guard that cannot fail guards nothing. These pin the scanner's behaviour
on the cases that matter.
Fixtures use r##"..."## because they embed r#"..."# source literals; a
single-hash outer string would terminate on the inner closing delimiter.
````

### tests/skill_paren_balance.rs:319

````text
The exact shape that shipped in PR #122: the final `result)` closes the
inner let, leaving procedure( open so the reader absorbs the rest.
````

### tests/skill_paren_balance.rs:377

````text
Regression guard: counting from the opening delimiter instead of the
content makes that quote blank the whole body and hide the defect.
````

### tests/tunnel_profile.rs:29

````text
Use the published vcli binary's transport helpers via the lib.
We can't easily call pub(crate) items from an integration test,
so we test the externally observable behavior: two profiles
resolve to two different setup dirs.
````

### tests/tunnel_profile.rs:58

````text
Simulate the cleanup-scope fix without a live SSH:
1. Create two fake profile setup dirs locally (the same way
they would exist on the remote after `tunnel start`).
2. Run a cleanup that scopes to ONE profile.
3. Assert the OTHER profile's dir is untouched.
The real `cleanup_remote()` runs over SSH; we test the path
resolution and scoping logic directly by calling the helper
and asserting the string we would `rm -rf`.
````


### tests/tunnel_profile.rs:118

````text
End-to-end: bind a profile to user-level, observe it via show,
then clear. Verifies the CLI plumbing works all the way through.
Redirect HOME to a scratch dir so the CLI's `~/.vcli` writes land in a
throwaway location. This test used to write the *real* `~/.vcli/.env`,
which both corrupted the developer's machine and made the assertions
depend on whatever happened to be there.
````
